name: Hypomyelination with atrophy of basal ganglia and cerebellum (H-ABC, TUBB4A)
aliases: hypomyelination with basal ganglia and cerebellar atrophy

clinicalPearls: A hypomyelinating leukodystrophy caused mainly by the recurrent de novo TUBB4A p.Asp249Asn variant, affecting a neuronal beta-tubulin isotype

The MRI pattern is highly recognisable: diffuse hypomyelination combined with progressive atrophy of the neostriatum, so that the putamen and caudate shrink and eventually seem to disappear, together with cerebellar atrophy
Children usually present in infancy or early childhood with motor delay, then evolve a mixed movement disorder of dystonia, rigidity, choreoathetosis and spasticity
Cerebellar signs (ataxia, dysarthria) and later cognitive involvement are common, and the extrapyramidal features tend to dominate the clinical picture
The disorder sits at the severe end of the TUBB4A spectrum, which also includes isolated hypomyelination and the dystonia syndrome DYT4 (whispering dysphonia)
Diagnosis is driven by pattern recognition on MRI followed by targeted TUBB4A sequencing; most cases are de novo but inherited variants occur
There is no curative treatment, so care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with attention to dystonia and spasticity management, nutrition, communication and physiotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: H-ABC is caused by pathogenic variants in TUBB4A, which encodes a beta-tubulin isotype highly expressed in the central nervous system. The altered tubulin disrupts microtubule dynamics and assembly, impairing processes that depend on the cytoskeleton in both oligodendrocytes and neurons. Defective oligodendrocyte function results in failure to lay down normal myelin (hypomyelination), while neuronal microtubule dysfunction contributes to degeneration of the striatum and cerebellum. The combination produces the characteristic imaging triad of hypomyelination with striatal and cerebellar atrophy and the accompanying extrapyramidal and cerebellar clinical features.
additionalDifferentials: Other TUBB4A-related phenotypes including isolated hypomyelinating leukodystrophy
Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies with basal ganglia involvement
Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy and other early-onset movement-disorder leukodystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to identify hypomyelination with neostriatal and cerebellar atrophy and to follow progression
TUBB4A sequencing, targeted first at the recurrent variant then broader analysis
Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy gene panel or exome if TUBB4A is negative
Metabolic screen to exclude treatable mimics (including neurotransmitter and organic acid studies)
Formal developmental and movement-disorder assessment to guide symptomatic therapy
Swallow and nutritional evaluation where feeding difficulty is present
redFlags: Status dystonicus with severe generalised dystonia, pain and metabolic derangement requiring urgent management
Progressive dysphagia with aspiration and faltering growth
Rapid neurological regression suggesting an intercurrent illness or alternative diagnosis
Respiratory compromise from bulbar and truncal involvement
reference.prognosis: H-ABC is progressive, with worsening movement disorder, spasticity and cognitive decline over childhood and adolescence; the striatal atrophy advances over time and many patients lose independent mobility. The severity and rate of decline vary with the specific variant, and life expectancy is reduced in more severely affected individuals, largely through bulbar and respiratory complications.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis by not recognising the disappearing putamen and caudate as a specific imaging clue
Attributing the movement disorder to cerebral palsy and not pursuing leukodystrophy imaging and genetics
Assuming autosomal recessive inheritance when most cases are de novo dominant variants
Neglecting proactive management of dystonia, which can escalate to status dystonicus
Failing to counsel families about recurrence risk, including germline mosaicism
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide symptomatic management of the mixed movement disorder, trialling agents for dystonia and rigidity such as levodopa, anticholinergics, baclofen and botulinum toxin injections
Treat spasticity with physiotherapy, oral antispasticity agents and, where severe, intrathecal baclofen
Support feeding and nutrition, with swallow assessment and gastrostomy where dysphagia threatens safe intake
Manage seizures with antiseizure medication if they occur
Provide multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation, communication aids and mobility support as the disease progresses
Monitor for aspiration, contractures and nutritional decline over the progressive course
Offer genetic counselling, noting most cases are de novo TUBB4A variants although inherited disease occurs
Introduce palliative and anticipatory care as motor and cognitive decline advances
